frictionVectors.title: EU energy dependence
frictionVectors.details: European demand for Algerian pipeline gas and LNG gives Algiers leverage, but regulatory pressure and energy-transition policies could reduce long-term dependence.

frictionVectors.title: Foreign competition in upstream investment
frictionVectors.details: Algeria is seeking investment from European, American and Asian firms while preserving Sonatrach’s dominant role, creating recurring disputes over terms and market access.

frictionVectors.title: Critical-minerals corridor competition
frictionVectors.details: The Lobito Corridor is drawing US, European and Gulf interest as an alternative to China-linked routes, increasing Angola’s leverage but also external pressure over infrastructure access.

frictionVectors.title: Debt and oil-sector exposure
frictionVectors.details: Heavy reliance on hydrocarbons and foreign financing constrains policy autonomy, while declining production and debt-service obligations remain major sovereignty risks.

frictionVectors.title: Port and logistics influence
frictionVectors.details: Cotonou’s strategic role attracts regional and foreign commercial interests, while dependence on external capital and neighboring markets limits Benin’s control over trade flows.

frictionVectors.title: Sahel spillover
frictionVectors.details: Militant activity along the northern borders is testing state capacity and could draw deeper security involvement from France, regional partners and other outside actors.

frictionVectors.title: De Beers renegotiation
frictionVectors.details: Botswana is pressing for greater value capture and domestic beneficiation from its diamond sector, creating tension with established foreign mining and marketing partners.

frictionVectors.title: Mineral diversification race
frictionVectors.details: Competition for copper, nickel and other strategic minerals is increasing external interest, but limited infrastructure and market scale constrain rapid diversification.

frictionVectors.title: Gold-sector nationalization
frictionVectors.details: Authorities are tightening control over artisanal and industrial gold production, challenging foreign mining firms while seeking greater state revenue and domestic processing.

frictionVectors.title: Russian security dependence
frictionVectors.details: Expanded security cooperation with Russia offers an alternative to Western support but risks new forms of dependency, opaque contracting and friction with regional and international institutions.

frictionVectors.title: Informal mineral trade
frictionVectors.details: Gold and other minerals move through opaque regional networks, limiting state revenues and enabling external traders to capture value.

frictionVectors.title: Border and aid dependency
frictionVectors.details: Economic pressure and dependence on external financing constrain policy autonomy, while instability around eastern Congo keeps border security sensitive.

frictionVectors.title: Foreign control of strategic infrastructure
frictionVectors.details: Port, airport, digital, and maritime-security projects rely heavily on foreign capital, creating long-term sovereignty and debt-management concerns.

frictionVectors.title: Maritime trafficking corridor
frictionVectors.details: The archipelago's location between West Africa, Europe, and the Americas exposes it to cocaine trafficking, illegal fishing, and pressure from external security partners.

highlights: Oil and timber revenues remain contested

frictionVectors.title: External capture of natural resources
frictionVectors.details: Foreign firms remain deeply embedded in oil, gas, mining, timber, and infrastructure, while opaque contracting and weak oversight limit domestic value retention.

frictionVectors.title: Conflict-affected transport corridors
frictionVectors.details: Violence in the Anglophone regions and Far North threatens roads, plantations, and trade routes, increasing reliance on outside security and humanitarian actors.

frictionVectors.title: Russian security-for-resources model
frictionVectors.details: Russian-linked security personnel retain major influence around regime protection and mining interests, limiting independent state control over strategic assets.

frictionVectors.title: Informal gold and diamond networks
frictionVectors.details: Weak administration and armed-group presence allow minerals to move through informal channels, depriving the treasury and sustaining external and local power brokers.

highlights: Sahel and Sudan pressures narrow autonomy

frictionVectors.title: Oil-sector dependence
frictionVectors.details: Hydrocarbon revenues and foreign technical and commercial partners dominate fiscal space, leaving the state vulnerable to price shocks and limited bargaining power.

frictionVectors.title: Sudan spillover and security partnerships
frictionVectors.details: The Sudan war is intensifying refugee, arms, and border-security pressures, while N'Djamena must balance ties with Western, Gulf, and regional security actors.

frictionVectors.title: French-Controlled Mayotte
frictionVectors.details: The unresolved status of Mayotte remains the central sovereignty issue, limiting Comoros' control over surrounding maritime space and migration policy. France retains decisive security and economic influence in the archipelago.

frictionVectors.title: External Infrastructure Finance
frictionVectors.details: Comoros depends heavily on foreign donors and diaspora transfers for ports, energy, and connectivity projects. This sustains basic development but leaves strategic infrastructure vulnerable to outside leverage.

frictionVectors.title: M23 and Regional Contestation
frictionVectors.details: Conflict in the east continues to undermine Kinshasa's territorial control and enables cross-border competition over trade routes, minerals, and security influence. Rwanda-linked allegations and broader regional involvement remain major flashpoints.

frictionVectors.title: Strategic Minerals Bargaining
frictionVectors.details: Copper and cobalt assets attract competing Chinese, Western, and Gulf interests, while weak enforcement limits the state's ability to capture full value. Contract renegotiation and processing ambitions are advancing but remain constrained by insecurity and infrastructure gaps.

frictionVectors.title: Hydrocarbon Dependence
frictionVectors.details: The state remains heavily dependent on offshore oil revenues, exposing public finances and sovereign leverage to price volatility and foreign-operator dominance. Limited diversification weakens long-term control over national resource wealth.

frictionVectors.title: Debt and Corridor Dependence
frictionVectors.details: Chinese-linked financing and construction remain important for roads, ports, and industrial projects. These ties improve connectivity but can narrow policy autonomy when debt service and project concessions compete with domestic priorities.

frictionVectors.title: Foreign Control of Cocoa Value
frictionVectors.details: Côte d'Ivoire is strengthening farmer pricing, traceability, and local processing, but multinational buyers and external standards still shape much of the cocoa economy. Capturing more downstream value remains a core sovereignty challenge.

frictionVectors.title: Port and Security Competition
frictionVectors.details: Abidjan's port and transport corridors attract competing French, Chinese, Gulf, and regional investment. Northern insecurity and dependence on external security partnerships could complicate efforts to control strategic trade routes.

frictionVectors.title: Foreign Military Footprint
frictionVectors.details: Djibouti monetizes its location through competing US, Chinese, French, Japanese, and other military facilities. The revenue and deterrence benefits come with heightened exposure to great-power rivalry and constrained strategic autonomy.

frictionVectors.title: Port Debt and Concessions
frictionVectors.details: China-linked financing and port infrastructure have expanded Djibouti's logistics role but increased debt and concession-related dependence. Regional competition with Gulf-backed facilities and Ethiopian trade needs further concentrates external leverage over the economy.

frictionVectors.title: Debt and Strategic-Asset Exposure
frictionVectors.details: Heavy borrowing from Gulf partners and international lenders has increased external influence over ports, logistics, and state assets. Cairo retains formal sovereignty but faces pressure to monetize strategic infrastructure.

frictionVectors.title: Nile Water Contest
frictionVectors.details: The GERD dispute with Ethiopia remains a core sovereignty and food-security concern. Unresolved negotiations leave Egypt exposed to shifts in Nile flows and regional alignment.

frictionVectors.title: Oil and Gas Dependence
frictionVectors.details: Declining hydrocarbon output and limited diversification constrain fiscal autonomy. Foreign operators, service firms, and lenders remain central to maintaining offshore production and LNG infrastructure.

frictionVectors.title: Maritime Boundary Pressure
frictionVectors.details: Offshore resource interests continue to shape relations with Cameroon, Gabon, and Nigeria. Maritime security and boundary management are increasingly important as existing fields mature.

frictionVectors.title: Foreign Mining Dependence
frictionVectors.details: Gold and base-metal projects provide hard currency but rely heavily on foreign capital, technology, and offtake arrangements. Limited transparency and sanctions exposure complicate long-term sovereign value capture.

frictionVectors.title: Red Sea Militarization
frictionVectors.details: Eritrea's coastline sits beside major shipping lanes and conflict zones, attracting competing regional and extra-regional security interests. Any expansion of port or military access could generate new diplomatic pressure.

frictionVectors.title: Customs and Energy Dependence
frictionVectors.details: Eswatini relies heavily on South African-linked customs revenue, electricity imports, transport routes, and market access. This gives Pretoria substantial indirect leverage over fiscal and infrastructure policy.

frictionVectors.title: Industrial Concession Pressure
frictionVectors.details: Textiles, sugar, and timber depend on external markets and preferential trade arrangements. Changes in US, regional, or European trade rules could quickly reduce domestic control over employment and export earnings.

frictionVectors.title: Nile Basin Confrontation
frictionVectors.details: The GERD strengthens Ethiopia's energy sovereignty but remains a major source of tension with Egypt and Sudan. Disputes over filling, operations, and data-sharing continue to carry regional escalation risks.

frictionVectors.title: External Finance and Corridor Access
frictionVectors.details: Debt restructuring, foreign-exchange shortages, and dependence on Djibouti-centered trade routes limit Addis Ababa's room for maneuver. Gulf, Chinese, Western, and regional actors are competing for influence over logistics, telecoms, and energy projects.

highlights: Military-led reset of mining and oil deals
Rail and port capacity remain strategic bottlenecks

frictionVectors.title: Contract renegotiation pressure
frictionVectors.details: The transitional authorities are seeking greater state participation and domestic processing in manganese, timber, and hydrocarbons, creating tension with established French and international operators.

frictionVectors.title: Transgabon Railway vulnerability
frictionVectors.details: The railway is vital for manganese exports and national connectivity, but aging infrastructure and dependence on external financing limit Gabon's control over its resource corridor.

highlights: Senegal remains the essential economic partner
Tourism and fisheries face external dependence

frictionVectors.title: Senegal-linked energy and trade dependence
frictionVectors.details: The Gambia relies heavily on Senegal for electricity interconnection, transport access, and regional supply chains, giving Dakar substantial structural leverage.

frictionVectors.title: Fisheries access disputes
frictionVectors.details: Foreign fishing activity and weak monitoring threaten local resource security, while opaque licensing and limited enforcement constrain sovereign control of maritime assets.

highlights: Gold anchors state revenue and foreign exchange
Debt restructuring is narrowing policy space

frictionVectors.title: Foreign-led mining and critical minerals
frictionVectors.details: International firms retain major influence over gold and emerging lithium projects, while Ghana is pressing for local value addition amid concerns over fiscal leakage and environmental damage.

frictionVectors.title: Illegal mining and water insecurity
frictionVectors.details: Galamsey continues to damage farmland and water systems, exposing gaps in enforcement and complicating efforts to present mining as a controlled national development strategy.

highlights: Simandou is reshaping Guinea's strategic weight

frictionVectors.title: Simandou external control
frictionVectors.details: Chinese-linked and international consortia are central to financing, building, and operating the Simandou iron-ore corridor, limiting immediate Guinean leverage despite ambitious local-content demands.

frictionVectors.title: Mining-sector political centralization
frictionVectors.details: The military government is using license reviews and infrastructure conditions to increase state control, raising uncertainty for foreign investors and tensions over labor and community benefits.

highlights: Cashew exports remain the economic lifeline

frictionVectors.title: Cashew-chain dependency
frictionVectors.details: Foreign traders and processors capture much of the value from Guinea-Bissau's cashew economy, while limited domestic processing leaves farmers and the state exposed to external price and logistics shocks.

frictionVectors.title: Bissau port and maritime insecurity
frictionVectors.details: Weak port capacity, political instability, and suspected narcotics networks undermine customs control and create openings for foreign commercial and security influence.

frictionVectors.title: External Debt and Port Leverage
frictionVectors.details: Debt-service pressures and reliance on external lenders continue to limit Nairobi's room to control strategic transport infrastructure. Competition among Chinese, Gulf, European, and Western partners around ports and logistics remains intense.

frictionVectors.title: Mining and Local Benefit Disputes
frictionVectors.details: New interest in critical minerals is attracting foreign capital faster than regulatory and community safeguards are developing. Disputes over licensing, royalties, land, and value addition could constrain sovereign resource gains.

frictionVectors.title: South African Water Dependence
frictionVectors.details: Lesotho's water exports and hydropower relationship with South Africa provide essential revenue but leave the kingdom structurally dependent on a larger neighbor. Disputes over pricing, project delays, and downstream infrastructure affect national bargaining power.

frictionVectors.title: Foreign-Owned Mining Exposure
frictionVectors.details: The diamond sector remains vulnerable to external ownership, volatile prices, and limited domestic processing. Revenue capture and labor benefits remain less secure than headline export values suggest.

highlights: Iron Ore and Port Stakes Rise

frictionVectors.title: Mining Concession Governance
frictionVectors.details: Foreign-led iron ore, gold, and prospective energy projects offer needed investment but continue to raise concerns over tax terms, land rights, environmental costs, and limited domestic value addition. Monrovia is seeking stronger oversight without deterring capital.

frictionVectors.title: Port and Corridor Competition
frictionVectors.details: Control and expansion of ports, rail links, and mining corridors are drawing competing foreign commercial interests. Liberia's infrastructure dependence reduces its leverage in negotiating long-term logistics and resource agreements.

frictionVectors.title: Fragmented Oil Governance
frictionVectors.details: Rival political and security networks continue to contest control over oil institutions, fields, terminals, and revenue flows. Production remains vulnerable to shutdowns used as leverage in domestic power struggles.

frictionVectors.title: Competing External Military Influence
frictionVectors.details: Turkey, Russia, Egypt, the United Arab Emirates, and European actors retain overlapping security and economic interests. Foreign military and logistical access complicates national reunification and weakens sovereign control of strategic infrastructure.

frictionVectors.title: Foreign-Controlled Mining Chains
frictionVectors.details: Nickel, cobalt, ilmenite, graphite, and other mineral projects remain dominated by foreign capital and export-oriented supply chains. Madagascar captures employment and fiscal benefits, but processing capacity and bargaining power remain limited.

frictionVectors.title: Land, Environment, and Infrastructure Conflict
frictionVectors.details: Mining corridors, ports, and energy projects generate recurring disputes over land access, water, biodiversity, and compensation. External investors and lenders have substantial influence over which infrastructure projects advance.

highlights: Debt restructuring opens limited fiscal space

frictionVectors.title: Mining Concessions and Strategic Minerals
frictionVectors.details: Government is seeking greater value capture from uranium, rare-earth, and other mineral projects, but financing and technical dependence leave negotiations vulnerable to foreign operators.

frictionVectors.title: Fuel and Power Dependence
frictionVectors.details: Foreign-exchange shortages, fuel-import exposure, and unreliable electricity constrain economic sovereignty and increase reliance on external lenders and infrastructure partners.

highlights: Junta tightens control over gold and mining
Russian security ties deepen strategic dependence

frictionVectors.title: Gold Governance and Foreign Operators
frictionVectors.details: Bamako is asserting stronger state participation and renegotiating mining terms, but insecurity and limited administrative capacity allow foreign firms and informal networks to retain substantial leverage.

frictionVectors.title: Sahel Security Realignment
frictionVectors.details: The relationship with Russia's Africa Corps has reduced Western influence but creates dependence on an external security provider while worsening tensions with regional and international institutions.

highlights: Iron ore remains vulnerable to logistics bottlenecks

frictionVectors.title: GTA Gas Project Governance
frictionVectors.details: The Senegal-Mauritania offshore gas project can expand state revenue and domestic energy access, but cross-border governance and reliance on multinational operators limit immediate sovereign control.

frictionVectors.title: Rail and Port Dependence
frictionVectors.details: Iron-ore exports remain concentrated around the SNIM rail corridor and Nouadhibou port, leaving national revenue exposed to external demand, transport costs, and infrastructure financing.

frictionVectors.title: Chagos and Diego Garcia Settlement
frictionVectors.details: The sovereignty dispute with the United Kingdom remains central to Mauritius's control of its maritime domain, while any settlement must balance national claims with the strategic role of the Diego Garcia base.

frictionVectors.title: Port and Maritime Competition
frictionVectors.details: India, China, and Western partners are competing for influence around Mauritius's ports, maritime surveillance, and logistics infrastructure, creating diversification opportunities but also strategic pressure.

highlights: Phosphate and renewables underpin strategic autonomy
Western Sahara remains the core sovereignty test

frictionVectors.title: Western Sahara Resource Diplomacy
frictionVectors.details: Rabat is using phosphate, fisheries, ports, and renewable-energy projects to consolidate control and attract investment, while recognition politics and legal disputes continue to challenge external legitimacy.

frictionVectors.title: Water and Energy Infrastructure
frictionVectors.details: Desalination, green hydrogen, and interconnection projects reduce vulnerability to imported energy and drought, but require substantial foreign capital, technology, and long-term offtake commitments.

frictionVectors.title: Cabo Delgado LNG Dependence
frictionVectors.details: Foreign-led LNG investment remains central to Mozambique’s fiscal ambitions, while insurgency and external security support limit fully sovereign control over the project zone.

frictionVectors.title: Port and Corridor Leverage
frictionVectors.details: Regional transport corridors and port development attract Gulf, Chinese, and Western capital, creating infrastructure gains but increasing dependence on external operators and financiers.

frictionVectors.title: Offshore Oil Contract Terms
frictionVectors.details: Recent offshore discoveries have strengthened Namibia’s bargaining position, but foreign majors retain substantial capital, technology, and operational leverage over future production.

frictionVectors.title: Green Hydrogen Financing
frictionVectors.details: Large hydrogen projects depend on European and other external financing, raising questions over local value capture, water use, and long-term export dependence.

frictionVectors.title: Uranium and Mining Realignment
frictionVectors.details: The military authorities are renegotiating relationships with Western mining interests while seeking alternative partners, creating uncertainty over production, revenue, and technical capacity.

frictionVectors.title: Oil Pipeline Vulnerability
frictionVectors.details: Niger’s export capacity remains exposed to political and security tensions along regional pipeline routes, especially where relations with neighboring transit states are strained.

frictionVectors.title: Pipeline Theft and Sabotage
frictionVectors.details: Crude theft, vandalism, and insecurity continue to reduce state revenues and weaken effective control over upstream assets despite regulatory reforms.

frictionVectors.title: Foreign Capital and Gas Bottlenecks
frictionVectors.details: Nigeria needs international capital and technology to expand oil and gas production, while weak infrastructure and contractual uncertainty limit domestic value capture.

frictionVectors.title: Critical Minerals Scrutiny
frictionVectors.details: Rwanda’s mineral-trading ambitions face international scrutiny over supply chains linked to eastern Democratic Republic of the Congo, threatening market access and diplomatic room.

frictionVectors.title: External Aid and Security Dependence
frictionVectors.details: Strong state capacity supports infrastructure and resource administration, but external aid, investment, and security partnerships remain important sources of strategic leverage.

frictionVectors.title: Gulf of Guinea Exposure
frictionVectors.details: Sao Tome and Principe remains dependent on external partners and regional security cooperation to police its maritime zone. Unproven offshore petroleum prospects create expectations without yet delivering sovereign revenue.

frictionVectors.title: External Finance Dependence
frictionVectors.details: Tourism, infrastructure, and public finances remain reliant on foreign donors and investors, limiting bargaining power over strategic assets and development priorities.

frictionVectors.title: Contract Renegotiation Pressure
frictionVectors.details: The government is seeking greater domestic value and fiscal returns from Sangomar and the Greater Tortue Ahmeyim gas project. Renegotiation efforts risk friction with international operators and financiers.

frictionVectors.title: Foreign Fishing Pressure
frictionVectors.details: Industrial and foreign-linked fishing fleets continue to challenge coastal communities and enforcement capacity. Fisheries depletion could become a major sovereignty issue alongside offshore hydrocarbons.

frictionVectors.title: Port Competition
frictionVectors.details: Seychelles must balance security and infrastructure relationships involving India, China, and other external partners. Port access and maritime surveillance cooperation can generate strategic dependency if not tightly managed.

frictionVectors.title: Tourism Concentration
frictionVectors.details: Heavy reliance on foreign tourism and imported goods leaves the economy exposed to external shocks. Climate impacts and sea-level rise further threaten control over maritime resources and critical infrastructure.

frictionVectors.title: Iron Ore Concession Exposure
frictionVectors.details: Large-scale iron ore operations and associated rail and port infrastructure give foreign-linked firms substantial influence over export logistics. Fiscal and local-content gains remain vulnerable to commodity cycles and opaque contracting.

frictionVectors.title: Coastal Resource Pressure
frictionVectors.details: Illegal and foreign-linked industrial fishing threatens artisanal livelihoods and state revenue. Limited monitoring capacity leaves coastal resources exposed to external exploitation.

frictionVectors.title: Somaliland-Ethiopia Dispute
frictionVectors.details: Ethiopian access arrangements with Somaliland challenge Mogadishu's territorial claims and could affect control of ports, maritime boundaries, and prospective offshore resources. The dispute also invites deeper Turkish, Gulf, and regional involvement.

frictionVectors.title: Security-Resource Linkage
frictionVectors.details: Al-Shabaab continues to constrain state control over transport corridors, agricultural land, and extractive prospects. Foreign security partnerships, including maritime and counterterrorism assistance, are essential but create long-term sovereignty trade-offs.

frictionVectors.title: MINING OWNERSHIP AND PROCESSING
frictionVectors.details: South Africa is seeking greater local beneficiation and leverage over platinum-group metals, manganese and other strategic minerals. Foreign capital remains essential, creating tension over ownership rules, export controls and industrial policy.

frictionVectors.title: ELECTRICITY AND LOGISTICS BOTTLENECKS
frictionVectors.details: Persistent weaknesses at Eskom, Transnet railways and ports reduce the state's ability to capture value from mining and manufacturing. Private operators and external financiers are gaining influence over infrastructure recovery.

highlights: Oil revenue remains the sovereignty hinge

frictionVectors.title: OIL CORRIDOR VULNERABILITY
frictionVectors.details: South Sudan remains heavily dependent on oil exports through Sudan, leaving revenue and production exposed to conflict, pipeline disruption and opaque intermediary arrangements. Foreign operators and neighboring transit authorities retain substantial leverage.

frictionVectors.title: ELITE CONTROL OF LAND AND SECURITY
frictionVectors.details: Competing political and military networks continue to control access to land, transport routes and natural resources. External security, humanitarian and commercial actors operate in a fragmented environment with limited national oversight.

highlights: Red Sea access becomes strategic prize

frictionVectors.title: GOLD AND WAR FINANCE
frictionVectors.details: Gold production and trafficking remain central to financing rival armed networks, with regional trading hubs and foreign intermediaries shaping access to hard currency. Formal state institutions have limited control over extraction and export channels.

frictionVectors.title: PORTS, PIPELINES AND EXTERNAL SPONSORS
frictionVectors.details: The Red Sea coast, oil infrastructure and transport corridors are exposed to competition among domestic factions and outside powers. Infrastructure access is increasingly negotiated through security relationships rather than unified national policy.

highlights: Ports and gas shape regional leverage

frictionVectors.title: LNG AND CONTRACT SOVEREIGNTY
frictionVectors.details: Tanzania is using negotiations over offshore gas development to secure stronger fiscal, domestic-supply and local-content terms. International energy companies and lenders still hold significant influence over project timing and commercial structure.

frictionVectors.title: PORT CORRIDOR COMPETITION
frictionVectors.details: Expansion of Dar es Salaam and proposed corridor projects is increasing Tanzania's regional leverage while inviting competition from foreign infrastructure investors and neighboring states. Debt, concession terms and local control remain politically sensitive.

highlights: Lomé consolidates Gulf of Guinea logistics

frictionVectors.title: PORT DEPENDENCE AND FOREIGN CAPITAL
frictionVectors.details: Lomé's role as a transshipment and landlocked-neighbor gateway gives Togo strategic revenue, but port operations and expansion remain dependent on foreign capital, operators and shipping networks. Disruptions or regulatory disputes could quickly affect national income.

frictionVectors.title: PHOSPHATE GOVERNANCE
frictionVectors.details: The phosphate sector remains a core sovereign asset, yet production, processing capacity and market access are constrained by financing and technical dependence. External partnerships can improve output while limiting domestic value capture.

frictionVectors.title: Migration-for-Finance Bargaining
frictionVectors.details: Tunisia remains dependent on European financial support and cooperation over irregular migration, giving external partners substantial influence over domestic priorities.

frictionVectors.title: Gas and Power Vulnerability
frictionVectors.details: Reliance on imported gas and electricity exposes Tunisia to supply disruptions and limits its strategic autonomy despite efforts to expand renewables.

frictionVectors.title: EACOP Financing Pressure
frictionVectors.details: The Lake Albert oil project and East African Crude Oil Pipeline remain central to Uganda's resource strategy, but financing, environmental opposition, and Western scrutiny constrain implementation.

frictionVectors.title: China-West Infrastructure Rivalry
frictionVectors.details: Uganda balances Chinese infrastructure and energy investment against Western financial and governance pressure, increasing the political cost of major strategic projects.

frictionVectors.title: Copper Ownership Contest
frictionVectors.details: Lusaka is seeking greater domestic value capture from copper while competing Chinese, Gulf, and Western investors pursue influence over mines, logistics, and processing capacity.

frictionVectors.title: Power and Rail Bottlenecks
frictionVectors.details: Electricity shortages and weak export corridors threaten mineral expansion, leaving Zambia dependent on external financing and neighboring transit routes.

frictionVectors.title: Critical Minerals Dependence
frictionVectors.details: Zimbabwe is tightening controls on unprocessed lithium and other minerals, but Chinese-linked firms retain a strong position in extraction, processing, and market access.

frictionVectors.title: Power and Currency Fragility
frictionVectors.details: Electricity shortages, currency instability, and restricted access to Western finance undermine state capacity to capture more value from mining revenues.
